title: Trace a packet from your machine to the internet
objective: By the end of this lesson you can follow one packet through address resolution and out to the internet, read an ARP table, and interpret the ICMP messages that tools like ping and traceroute are actually built on.

blocks.text: You now know how a machine picks a next hop. This lesson closes the gap between that decision and the wire: a routing table gives you an IP address, but a network card can only address a device by its hardware address. Something has to translate. That something is ARP, and watching it work is the clearest way to see the boundary between the network layer and the link layer.
The full path of one packet

items: Your program calls connect() to a public address
The routing table says: not on my network, send it to the gateway
The link layer needs the gateway's hardware address — does the ARP table have it?
If not, broadcast: 'who has 192.0.2.1?' to every device on the segment
The gateway alone replies with its hardware address; the answer is cached
The frame goes out addressed to the gateway's hardware address, but carrying the far destination's IP address
The gateway strips the frame, looks up its own routing table, and repeats all of this on its next link

blocks.title: The destination IP never changes; the destination MAC changes every hop
blocks.text: This is the single most clarifying fact about the two layers. The IP address in the packet is where it is ultimately going, and stays constant end to end. The hardware address on the frame is only ever the next device on this particular wire, and is rewritten at every hop. If you understand that sentence, you understand the relationship between the network layer and the link layer.

blocks.caption: Entries from a real table, with what each kind means
lines: 192.0.2.255      ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff    <- broadcast: every device accepts it
224.0.0.251      01:00:5e:00:00:fb    <- multicast, and computed rather than asked
/* Only the first was learned over the network. The others follow rules. */

blocks.title: Multicast hardware addresses are calculated, not resolved
blocks.text: For an IPv4 multicast group, the hardware address is 01:00:5e followed by the low 23 bits of the IP address. Verified against a live table: 224.0.0.251 gives 01:00:5e:00:00:fb, and 239.255.255.250 gives 01:00:5e:7f:ff:fa — both match exactly. No query is needed, because both ends can compute the same answer. This is also why the mapping is not unique: several IP groups can collapse onto one hardware address, and the receiver filters the rest out in software.

An ARP reply is believed because it arrived. Nothing in the protocol proves that the responder is the machine it claims to be, so any device on the segment can answer for any address. That is the basis of ARP spoofing: an attacker answers 'I am the gateway', your machine caches it, and your traffic goes through the attacker before reaching the real gateway.

It is worth being precise about the scope of that risk. It requires the attacker to already be on your local segment — it is not something reachable from across the internet. It is a serious risk on shared or untrusted networks, and it is a large part of why traffic is encrypted end to end: an attacker who reroutes a TLS connection still cannot read it, and cannot impersonate the server without a certificate the browser will accept.
ICMP: the network reporting on itself
ICMP is not a transport for your data. It is how the network tells a sender what happened. The numbers below are as published by IANA.

rows: Hop limit ran out — this is what traceroute uses
Route exists, machine did not answer
Nothing listening on that UDP port
Packet too large for a link — the MTU message from the layers lesson

blocks.title: How traceroute actually works
blocks.text: It sends packets with the hop limit set to 1, then 2, then 3. Each router that decrements the limit to zero discards the packet and reports Time Exceeded — type 11, code 0 — and that reply reveals the router's address. The path is discovered one hop at a time by deliberately sending packets that cannot arrive. That also explains the stars: a router configured not to send these replies stays invisible while still forwarding traffic normally.

blocks.title: Blocking all ICMP breaks more than ping
blocks.text: A firewall rule that drops ICMP entirely also drops type 3 code 4 — the message that tells a sender its packets are too large. The result is the failure from the layers lesson: small requests succeed, large ones hang, and nothing in any log explains it. Block echo requests if you must, but permit destination-unreachable and time-exceeded.

blocks.title: Follow one packet all the way out
steps: Run: ip neigh    (or arp -an) and identify your gateway's entry
Delete it: sudo ip neigh flush all      then run ping -c 1 <gateway> and check that it reappeared
In one terminal run: sudo tcpdump -n -i any arp     and in another, flush and ping again — you should see the query and the reply
Identify any multicast entries and verify the 01:00:5e rule by hand for one of them
Run: ping -c 2 <a public address>   under tcpdump -n icmp and identify the echo request and reply by type
Run: traceroute -n 1.1.1.1   under the same capture and find the time-exceeded messages
Run: nc -u -z <your own address> 9999   and look for a port-unreachable message

Run: ping -c 1 -M do -s 2000 1.1.1.1   — the 2000-byte packet exceeds your interface's 1500-byte MTU with DF set, so it fails locally: ping reports 'Message too long' (EMSGSIZE) and nothing is sent. Interpret that local error — your own kernel refusing the send, not an ICMP reply. To actually capture type 3 code 4 you need a path MTU smaller than your interface MTU: repeat the command through a VPN or PPPoE tunnel and capture again
blocks.expected: An ARP exchange you triggered yourself, a multicast address whose hardware address you computed and then confirmed, and captures showing echo, time-exceeded and port-unreachable messages. The oversized DF-set ping ends in a local 'Message too long' error — the packet never left your machine, so no ICMP reply can appear, and recognising that local failure is itself the exercise. Seeing a real fragmentation-needed message requires a path with a smaller MTU, such as a VPN or PPPoE tunnel, where the same command produces the type 3 code 4 reply on the wire.

cheatsheet: The destination IP is constant end to end; the destination MAC changes at every hop
ARP asks the whole segment 'who has this IP' and caches the reply
ip neigh (or arp -an) shows the cache
Multicast MAC is 01:00:5e plus the low 23 bits of the IP — computed, never asked
ARP has no authentication — spoofing requires local access but is easy once there
ICMP types: 0 echo reply, 3 unreachable, 5 redirect, 8 echo request, 11 time exceeded
Type 3 codes: 0 net, 1 host, 2 protocol, 3 port, 4 fragmentation needed
traceroute works by sending packets with a hop limit of 1, 2, 3 and reading the time-exceeded replies
Never block ICMP wholesale: type 3 code 4 is what prevents the silent large-packet hang

checkpoint.prompt: A packet leaves your machine for a server on another continent. What is in the frame's destination hardware address field?

choices.A: It is left empty until the packet reaches the internet

checkpoint.explanation: The next device on this wire. The IP address is the final destination and never changes. The hardware address is only ever the next hop, and is rewritten by every router along the way.

checkpoint.prompt: Your ARP table contains 224.0.0.251 mapped to 01:00:5e:00:00:fb. How was that mapping obtained?

choices.A: It was computed from the IP address
choices.B: From the DHCP server when it assigned the address

checkpoint.explanation: Verified against a live table for two different groups. Both ends can calculate the same answer, so no query is needed. Multicast hardware addresses are computed as 01:00:5e plus the low 23 bits of the IP address.

checkpoint.prompt: An administrator blocks all ICMP at the firewall. Users report that small web pages load but large downloads hang. Why?

choices.A: ICMP destination-unreachable with code 4 is blocked
choices.B: The connection limit was reached and new transfers are refused
choices.D: The firewall is dropping TCP too

checkpoint.explanation: This is the layers lesson's MTU failure with a cause you can now name. Blocking echo requests is a defensible choice; blocking destination-unreachable is not. Type 3 code 4 is fragmentation needed: without it, senders never learn their packets are too large.

checkpoint.prompt: How does traceroute discover the routers along a path?

choices.A: It sends packets with increasing hop limits
choices.B: It reads the routing tables remotely
choices.C: It uses DNS records for each hop
choices.D: It asks each router to report its neighbours and next hops

checkpoint.explanation: Each router that discards one reports Time Exceeded, revealing its address. The path is mapped by deliberately sending packets that cannot arrive. A router configured not to send those replies appears as a star while still forwarding traffic normally. Concretely, it sends hop limits of 1, then 2, then 3, and so on.
